Day 80 of 100 · Kubernetes

Kubernetes Ingress

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityKubernetesPublished artifact recovered

Ingress describes HTTP/HTTPS routing rules toward Services; an Ingress controller is the component that actually implements those rules.

Architecture / mental model

external client → Ingress controller → Service → Ready Pods

How it works

A Service provides a stable endpoint for Pods, while Ingress adds HTTP-aware routing such as host and path rules in front of Services.

The Ingress resource is configuration. A controller watches those resources and configures a proxy/load balancer to implement them. Creating an Ingress object without a compatible controller does not expose the application.

IngressClass and controller selection matter in clusters with multiple controllers or explicit class requirements. TLS configuration also introduces certificate/secret ownership and termination decisions.

Hands-on reference

kubectl get ingressclass
kubectl get ingress
kubectl describe ingress web
kubectl get svc
kubectl get endpointslices

Verification

Resolve the hostname to the intended ingress endpoint, send an HTTP/HTTPS request and trace the path from controller to Service to EndpointSlices/Pods. Confirm the controller actually observed the resource.

Field note / gotcha

An Ingress resource with no controller is basically a very confident routing wish.

Security considerations

Terminate TLS deliberately, protect certificate Secrets, restrict controller privileges and use NetworkPolicy/backend controls instead of assuming the ingress boundary alone secures workloads.

What I learned

Kubernetes separates the desired routing rule from the component that implements it, and debugging must keep those two objects distinct.
